passage: All through maths, Xin kept glancing at the clock. That morning in their Vancouver apartment, Mum had stayed in bed with a fever and a cough, her voice croaky. 'Go to school, sweetheart. I'll be fine.' But what if she wasn't? Xin got three sums wrong that she usually knew. At lunch she couldn't finish her dumplings. Mr Santiago noticed and crouched by her desk. 'You seem far away today.' Xin's eyes stung. 'My mum's sick.' He nodded. 'That's a hard thing to carry at school. Want to call her at break from the office?' She did. Mum sounded sleepy but okay. 'Can I help when I get home?' Xin asked. 'Make me some warm honey water. And tell me about your day.'

qa.q: What could Xin not finish at lunch?
qa.a: Her dumplings.

qa.q: Why did Xin keep glancing at the clock?
qa.a: She was worried about Mum, who was sick at home, and anxious that she might not be fine.

qa.q: What helped Xin cope with the worry?
qa.a: Telling Mr Santiago, calling Mum at break, and asking how she could help, instead of carrying it alone.

qa.q: How might Mum feel when Xin asks how to help?
qa.a: Touched and cared for; she gives Xin a small job and a chat, not a big responsibility 🙂

grounding: A girl worries about her sick mother all day at school, tells her teacher, and asks her mother how she can help.

passage: Neelam stood outside the staffroom, twisting her ID card string. Amma had been in hospital since Sunday for an operation, and Neelam hadn't slept well since. She knocked. 'Chandrika Ma'am, can I skip basketball practice today? And maybe the test?' Ma'am put down her pen. 'Tell me what's going on.' Neelam told her. The words tumbled out: the hospital, the waiting, how she kept thinking she should be there, helping Amma get better. Ma'am listened, then said gently, 'Making her better is the doctors' job, not yours. Your job is being her daughter.' They agreed Neelam would take the test later but still go to practice, because running always cleared her head. That evening she told Amma about her three baskets, and Amma smiled for the first time in days.

qa.q: Since when had Amma been in hospital?
qa.a: Since Sunday.

qa.q: What did Neelam's twisting of her ID card string show?
qa.a: She was nervous and worried, carrying her fear about Amma and feeling she should be helping her get better.

qa.q: What did Ma'am help Neelam decide?
qa.a: To take the test later but keep going to practice, which clears her head, and to leave the healing to the doctors.

qa.q: How might Amma feel hearing about the three baskets?
qa.a: Cheered and proud; she smiled for the first time in days.

grounding: At school a girl worried about her mother in hospital tells a teacher, keeps her routine and lets go of trying to cure her.

passage: Last winter my brother Siddharth had bad asthma attacks, and our whole house turned around him. Mummy slept in his room. Papa rushed home early with his medicines. Nobody came to my annual day, where I was the lead tree in the play. I'm Bhavna, and I remember thinking, I wish I were sick too. Then I felt awful, because some nights Siddharth could hardly breathe. One evening I told Papa both things: that I was jealous, and that I felt terrible for being jealous. He didn't get angry. He said both feelings made sense. After that, Papa and I had Sunday mornings for just the two of us, making poha together. And I read comics to Siddharth when he was stuck in bed.

qa.q: What part did Bhavna play at annual day?
qa.a: The lead tree in the play.

qa.q: What two feelings did Bhavna have about Siddharth's illness?
qa.a: Jealous of all the attention he got, and then guilty for feeling that while he could hardly breathe.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do with those feelings?
qa.a: Bhavna told Papa honestly, got Sunday mornings alone with him, and still read comics to Siddharth.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt hearing Bhavna's confession?
qa.a: Understanding, and perhaps sorry Bhavna had felt left out, since he said both feelings made sense and made time for them.

grounding: A child feels jealous of a sick brother's attention and then guilty, asks a parent for time, and still cares for the brother.

passage:
Class teacher's note, 4C, Wednesday.
During art, the class made get-well cards for Harish, Raghav's younger brother, who has been in hospital for two weeks. Raghav drew nothing. When I asked, he muttered, 'Everyone's always making things for Harish. Nobody even asked about my football final.' Then his face went red and he covered it. 'I'm horrible. He's sick and I'm jealous.' I told him that jealous and guilty can sit side by side in anyone, and neither makes him bad. I suggested he tell his parents he misses time with them. He decided to make Harish a card with a football on it, 'so he knows about my final too.' I have emailed his mother about our chat.

qa.q: How long has Harish been in hospital?
qa.a: Two weeks.

qa.q: Why did Raghav cover his red face?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and guilty for being jealous of Harish while Harish was sick.

qa.q: What did the teacher suggest, and what did Raghav decide?
qa.a: To tell his parents he misses time with them; Raghav chose to make Harish a card with a football on it.

qa.q: How might Harish feel getting a football card from Raghav?
qa.a: Happy and included, hearing about his brother's final even from hospital.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a boy admitting jealousy and guilt about his sick brother, and turning it into care.

passage: Ritu had been in the district hospital in Sitapur for five days with typhoid. Every evening, when the bus brought Amma home, Aparna handed her a new drawing for Ritu: the goats, the neem tree, their cat asleep on the grain sack. 'She stuck the cat on the wall by her bed,' Amma reported. On Saturday, the neighbours' children called Aparna to play gilli-danda in the lane. She hesitated at the door. How could she laugh while her little sister lay in a hospital bed? Dadi, shelling peas on the step, looked up. 'Go. Being sad all day won't make her well faster. Play, and then draw her the game.' Aparna played till dusk. That night she drew the gilli flying over the lane, with Ritu cheering from the side.

qa.q: What did Ritu stick on the wall by her bed?
qa.a: The drawing of the cat.

qa.q: Why did Aparna hesitate at the door?
qa.a: She felt guilty about laughing and playing while her little sister lay in a hospital bed.

qa.q: What did Dadi help Aparna see?
qa.a: That being sad all day won't help Ritu; she can play and still show care by drawing the game for her.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel getting Aparna's drawings?
qa.a: Cheered and connected to home; she even stuck the cat drawing on the wall 😊

grounding: A village girl draws pictures for her sister in hospital and learns she may play without guilt.

passage: Emil's little sister Hana had been in the children's hospital in Copenhagen for two weeks. Every afternoon Emil sat at the kitchen table with his felt-tip pens and drew her something: a whale, a rocket, their dog in a raincoat. Mum took the pictures in when she visited. On Friday his friend invited him to a birthday party at the swimming pool. Emil said no. 'It feels wrong to have fun,' he told Dad. Dad sat down. 'Hana asked me yesterday if you were still going to parties. She wants to hear about them. It's okay to be sad and to have fun in the same week.' Emil went. Afterwards he drew Hana a picture of himself on the big slide, with a speech bubble: 'Next time, you too.'

qa.q: What did Emil draw for Hana after the party?
qa.a: A picture of himself on the big slide, with a speech bubble.

qa.q: Why did Emil first say no to the party?
qa.a: He felt guilty about having fun while Hana was in hospital.

qa.q: What did Dad help Emil understand?
qa.a: That it's okay to be sad and to have fun in the same week, and that Hana wants to hear about his fun.

qa.q: What might Hana want from her brother while she is in hospital?
qa.a: To hear about his life and still feel part of it, which is why she asked about parties.

grounding: A boy whose little sister is in hospital draws for her and learns that having fun is not a betrayal.

passage: The community hall was full of wedding lights and the smell of halwa, and Siddharth had been bouncing since breakfast. His cousins from Amritsar had arrived! He dragged Gurpreet and three smaller cousins to the corner where he'd hidden his box of cars. 'Okay, rules. I'm the race boss. Gurpreet, you're only allowed the blue truck. You little ones just watch.' Within five minutes the little ones had wandered off, and Gurpreet was sitting on the stage steps, chin in his hands. Siddharth's excitement drained away. This wasn't how he'd imagined it. He picked up the box and walked over. 'Sorry. Everybody picks one car. And you choose the track.' Gurpreet grinned and built a ramp from a chair cushion, and the little ones came running back.

qa.q: Where had Siddharth hidden his box of cars?
qa.a: In the corner of the community hall.

qa.q: What happened to Siddharth's excitement after five minutes, and why?
qa.a: It drained into disappointment, because bossing everyone around made them leave.

qa.q: What fixed the game?
qa.a: Apologising, letting everyone pick a car and letting Gurpreet choose the track.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel about being allowed only the blue truck?
qa.a: Bored and left out, so he sat on the stage steps with his chin in his hands.

grounding: A boy excited about visiting cousins spoils the fun by bossing, then shares and includes everyone.

passage:
Friday. Mridul counted the hours until his cousin Sonali's train came in from Jaipur. He'd made a list and stuck it on the fridge: kite flying, the water park, a ghost story night.
Sunday. By the second day, Mridul was bossing. 'No, we're doing the list in order. You can't just play carrom.' Sonali went quiet and sat with Nani, shelling peanuts. Mridul felt a strange hollow in his stomach. He had wanted this for months, so why wasn't it fun?
Tuesday. Mridul tore the list in half. 'Your half,' he said, handing it over. 'You pick.' Sonali picked carrom first. He lost three games in a row and laughed harder than he had all week.

qa.q: What was on Mridul's list?
qa.a: Kite flying, the water park and a ghost story night.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when the strange hollow came into his stomach?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and uneasy, sensing that his bossing was spoiling the visit he had been so excited about.

qa.q: What did Mridul do on Tuesday that brought the fun back?
qa.a: He tore the list in half and let Sonali choose, sharing the plans instead of ordering her around.

qa.q: What was it like for Sonali on Sunday?
qa.a: She felt pushed around and left out, so she went quiet and sat with Nani.

grounding: Over several days a boy excited for his cousin's visit learns that bossing ruins the fun and sharing brings it back.

passage: At Bua's flat in Dwarka, Sunday lunch was loud and full of rajma. Then Phoopha-ji asked the question. 'Nitin, how many marks in maths?' 'Seventy-two.' 'Sarita got ninety-eight,' Bua said, beaming. 'Learn from your cousin, beta.' Everyone nodded. Nitin stared at his plate. He felt about two inches tall. Sarita's ears were red, and she was pushing rice into a little wall. On the metro home, Nitin said quietly, 'Papa, I hate it when they do that. I felt so small.' Papa put an arm around him. 'You're not a number. I'll tell Bua we don't do comparisons.' Nitin nodded. Then he thought of Sarita's red ears. Maybe being the one held up wasn't fun either.

qa.q: What marks did Nitin get in maths?
qa.a: Seventy-two.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel when Bua told him to learn from his cousin?
qa.a: Small and hurt, about two inches tall, as he stared at his plate.

qa.q: What did Nitin do after lunch that helped?
qa.a: He told Papa honestly that he felt small, and Papa reassured him and offered to speak to Bua.

qa.q: What might Sarita have felt during the comparison?
qa.a: Embarrassed and uncomfortable; her red ears and the rice wall suggest she felt judged too.

grounding: A boy feels small when relatives compare his marks with his cousin's, tells his father, and sees his cousin may feel judged too.

passage:
'Did you hear Masi?' Eshaan kicked the terrace wall. '"Ankita came first again, Eshaan, what happened to you?" In front of everyone.'
Ankita leaned on the railing. 'I heard.'
'You don't get it. You're always the good example.'
'You think that's fun?' Ankita said. 'Now if I come second, everyone will say, "What happened to Ankita?" I couldn't even eat my gulab jamun.'
Eshaan stared. 'Really?'
'Really. I'm not a rank either.'
They were quiet. Then Eshaan said, 'I'm going to tell Mummy it made me feel rubbish.'
'Tell her to ask Masi to stop, for both of us.'
Downstairs, Eshaan found Mummy by the sweets table. 'Can we talk? Masi's comparing thing hurt.' Mummy put her plate down. 'Come. I'm listening.'

qa.q: What could Ankita not eat?
qa.a: Her gulab jamun.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel after Masi's comment?
qa.a: Hurt and humiliated at being compared in front of everyone, so he kicked the terrace wall.

qa.q: What step did Eshaan take after talking with Ankita?
qa.a: He told Mummy the comparison hurt, and she put her plate down to listen.

qa.q: How does Ankita experience being the good example?
qa.a: As pressure, not fun; she worries what people will say if she ever comes second.

grounding: A boy hurt by a relative comparing his marks with his cousin's learns she feels judged too, and tells his mother.

passage:
From Nani's holiday notebook, Tuesday.
Pankaj and Nikita played cricket in the courtyard all afternoon. Pankaj kept count loudly: 'Twenty-three runs to your eleven!' When Nikita hit a six over the tulsi, he claimed it was out. Later, doing holiday homework, he kept peeking at her page and racing to finish first. Tonight he sulked because she knew the capital of Peru and he didn't. I called him into the kitchen. 'Do you want to play with Nikita, or beat her?' He thought, then said, 'Both. But mostly beat.' I asked him what she does well. 'She bowls spin better than me,' he admitted. Tomorrow he has asked her to teach him the googly. I'll watch how it goes.

qa.q: What did Nikita know that Pankaj didn't?
qa.a: The capital of Peru.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj claim Nikita's six was out?
qa.a: He felt threatened and jealous, wanting so badly to be better that he couldn't bear her doing well.

qa.q: What question from Nani helped Pankaj, and what did he decide?
qa.a: 'Do you want to play with Nikita, or beat her?'; he decided to ask her to teach him the googly.

qa.q: How might Nikita feel when her six was called out?
qa.a: Annoyed and unfairly treated, since the six was a good hit.

grounding: A grandmother's notebook shows a boy's rivalry with his cousin turning unfair, and a question that turns it towards learning from her.

passage:
Sunday
Dear diary, Darshan writing. Jasleen came for the weekend again, and I spent the whole time trying to beat her. Swimming race at the club: she won by a whole arm. Then Chachi asked about the maths olympiad, and Jasleen had a gold certificate and I had silver. I went quiet all through dinner. Tonight I noticed something ugly. When Jasleen dropped her ice cream, I was glad. Glad! That's not who I want to be. It's fine to want to be good, but wanting her to fall is something else. Tomorrow I'm going to ask how she learnt that flip turn at the wall. Maybe if I learn from her instead of racing her every second, I'll actually get faster.

qa.q: Who won the swimming race?
qa.a: Jasleen, by a whole arm.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel on noticing the gladness about the dropped ice cream?
qa.a: Ashamed and uneasy, seeing that the rivalry had turned into wanting Jasleen to fail.

qa.q: What plan does Darshan make for tomorrow?
qa.a: To ask Jasleen how she learnt her flip turn, learning from her instead of racing her every second.

qa.q: How might Jasleen see Darshan's quiet dinner?
qa.a: She might feel confused or uneasy, unsure why her gold certificate made her cousin go silent.

grounding: A child writes about a rivalry with a cousin, notices wanting her to fail, and decides to learn from her strengths.

passage: Every summer at Nani's house in Lucknow, my older cousins Amandeep and Farah shut themselves in the back room with their card games. I'm Imran, the youngest by three years, and I used to stand outside the door listening to them laugh. That summer I tried something new. I knocked and said, 'Can I play? I learnt rummy.' Farah said, 'You'll slow us down.' It stung. I tried again. 'What if we play something for three, like ludo?' Amandeep shrugged, but Farah shut the door. So I went to the courtyard and played marbles with my little cousin Zaid, which was actually fun. At dinner I told Nani, calmly, 'They never let me in.' Nani didn't fuss. The next day she set up a family carrom match and put me on Amandeep's team.

qa.q: What game did Imran suggest for three?
qa.a: Ludo.

qa.q: How did Imran feel when Farah said 'You'll slow us down'?
qa.a: Stung and left out, after trying hard to join.

qa.q: Which steps did Imran try, and which worked?
qa.a: Asking to join and suggesting a game for three didn't work; playing with Zaid and calmly telling Nani did, and Nani set up a family carrom match.

qa.q: Why might Farah want to keep the room to herself?
qa.a: She may enjoy time with a cousin her own age and see Imran as too young, without noticing how it hurts.

grounding: A child left out by two older cousins asks to join, suggests a game, plays with another cousin and calmly tells a grandparent.

passage:
Note to Didi, from Sangeeta Mami, after the mehendi night.
I wanted you to know how Pallavi handled the evening. Kavita and Juhi, the older cousins, spent the whole night whispering and practising their own dance, and turned their backs whenever Pallavi came near. I watched her try. She asked, 'Can I learn the steps?' They said, 'Later.' She suggested all three of them play musical chairs. No. Her lip wobbled. Then she found little Manav by the henna table, and they made up a silly dance together. Near midnight she came to me and said quietly, 'Kavita and Juhi keep leaving me out.' No tears, no drama. I thanked her for telling me and spoke to the girls. Kavita taught her the steps before breakfast.

qa.q: Who did Pallavi dance with by the henna table?
qa.a: Little Manav.

qa.q: What did Pallavi's wobbling lip show?
qa.a: She felt hurt and left out after asking twice and being turned away.

qa.q: How did Pallavi handle being excluded?
qa.a: She asked to join, suggested a game, played with Manav, and calmly told Mami, who spoke to the older girls.

qa.q: How might Kavita see the evening?
qa.a: Mostly as fun with Juhi, perhaps not noticing how left out Pallavi felt until Mami spoke to her.

grounding: An aunt's note describes a girl left out by older cousins at a family function who tries to join, plays with a younger cousin and calmly tells an adult.

passage: Last Diwali holidays my small cousin Kunal came to stay with us in Indore. He is six and has a stammer. On the second evening, three boys from the next building copied him outside the gate: 'K-k-k-Kunal!' He froze with his sparkler box, face crumpling. My blood went hot. I'm Ganga, and part of me wanted to shove the biggest boy into the drain. Instead I walked over and stood right beside Kunal, my hand on his shoulder. 'He's my cousin. Stop it,' I said, as steadily as I could. One boy laughed and started again. So I said, 'Fine, I'm calling my uncle,' and shouted for Chacha from the gate. Chacha came down at once, and the boys left. Kunal held my hand all evening.

qa.q: What was Kunal holding when the boys teased him?
qa.a: His sparkler box.

qa.q: What did Ganga feel when the boys copied Kunal?
qa.a: Angry and protective; Ganga's blood went hot, and part of Ganga wanted to shove the biggest boy.

qa.q: Which steps did Ganga take instead of fighting?
qa.a: Standing beside Kunal, speaking steadily, and calling Chacha when the teasing continued.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt with Ganga beside him?
qa.a: Safer and less alone; he held Ganga's hand all evening.

grounding: A child protects a small cousin from teasing by standing beside him, speaking calmly and fetching an adult.

passage:
Note from Himani Joshi, tuition teacher, to Hemant's parents.
From my balcony this evening I saw something you should know about. Some older boys in the park were grabbing your nephew Bittu's cap and tossing it over his head while he jumped for it, crying. Hemant ran over from the swings. He didn't shout or push. He stood in front of Bittu and said, 'Give it back. He's four.' His voice was shaking a little, but he kept looking at the tallest boy. When they kept tossing it, Hemant took Bittu's hand and walked straight to the guard's cabin. The guard got the cap back and sent the boys off. Hemant chose calm over a fight. I thought you would want to know.

qa.q: Where did Hemant take Bittu when the boys kept tossing the cap?
qa.a: Straight to the guard's cabin.

qa.q: What does Hemant's shaking voice suggest?
qa.a: He was nervous and scared of the older boys, but protective enough to keep standing in front of Bittu.

qa.q: Why was going to the guard a wise step?
qa.a: The teasing kept going, so fetching an adult solved it without a fight.

qa.q: What was it like for Bittu when the boys took his cap?
qa.a: Frightening and upsetting; he was crying and jumping for it, so Hemant's help probably felt like a rescue.

grounding: A tuition teacher's note describes a boy protecting his small cousin from older boys calmly and fetching an adult.

passage:
Note by Usha Menon, Class 6 teacher, Monday.
At lunch today I saw Bhavna carry her tray to the corner table where four girls sit. One of them put her bag on the empty chair and said, 'There's no place for you here.' The others laughed. Bhavna stood for a moment, then walked to the steps and ate nothing. Afterwards she came to me, eyes wet. 'They always do this,' she said. I thanked her for telling me and said it said nothing bad about her. I spoke to the four girls straight after lunch. I also introduced Bhavna to Lavanya, who usually eats alone with a book, and mentioned our Tuesday nature club. I called Bhavna's mother this evening and will watch that table all week.

qa.q: What did one girl put on the empty chair?
qa.a: Her bag.

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel after being turned away, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Deeply hurt; she ate nothing on the steps and came to the teacher with wet eyes.

qa.q: What steps did the teacher take the same day?
qa.a: Spoke to the four girls, introduced Bhavna to Lavanya, mentioned the nature club and called her mother that evening.

qa.q: What might Lavanya feel when Bhavna is introduced?
qa.a: Perhaps glad of company, since she usually eats alone with a book.

grounding: A teacher's note records a girl turned away by a group at lunch, telling the teacher, and the same-day steps taken.

passage:
Thursday
Diary, it's Bidisha. Today at recess I asked Ishani's group if I could sit with them, and Ishani said, 'Sorry, table's full,' even though there were two empty spaces. They all went quiet till I walked away. My whole chest hurt. I ate in the library. But Shreya was there too, drawing horses, and she pushed her sketchbook over and said, 'Help me with the legs?' We laughed at my wonky horse. She's joining the choir next week and asked me to come. Tonight I told Ma about the table. She didn't say 'just ignore them.' She hugged me and said she'd talk to my class teacher tomorrow morning. I still feel sad. But I also have a horse-drawing friend now.

qa.q: Where did Bidisha eat after being turned away?
qa.a: In the library.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel when Ishani said the table was full?
qa.a: Deeply hurt and rejected; Bidisha's whole chest hurt.

qa.q: What helped Bidisha after the rejection?
qa.a: Finding Shreya, a kind classmate, planning to join the choir, and telling Ma, who hugged Bidisha and promised to talk to the class teacher.

qa.q: How might Shreya see Bidisha turning up in the library?
qa.a: As welcome company; she shared her sketchbook and invited Bidisha to choir 🙂

grounding: A child writes about being turned away by a group, finding one kind classmate and a club, and telling a parent.

passage:
Monday. Reena watched the popular girls laughing by the water cooler, all with matching butterfly clips. She bought the same clips with her pocket money and practised their giggle in the mirror.
Wednesday. Usha, the leader, finally waved her over. 'You can hang out with us. But first, go tell Ruchi her lunch stinks. Loudly.' Ruchi was sitting alone, eating poha. Reena's stomach twisted. She had wanted this for months.
Thursday. Reena didn't go to the water cooler. She sat down next to Ruchi. 'Your poha smells nice, actually. Is there onion in it?' Ruchi looked up, surprised, and smiled. Reena took the butterfly clips out of her hair and put them in her pencil box. She didn't feel sorry at all.

qa.q: What did the popular girls wear?
qa.a: Matching butterfly clips.

qa.q: Why did Reena's stomach twist on Wednesday?
qa.a: She was torn: she envied the group and wanted in, but being cruel to Ruchi felt wrong.

qa.q: What was the wise choice on Thursday, and why?
qa.a: Sitting with Ruchi instead of joining; belonging that required cruelty cost too much.

qa.q: What might Ruchi have felt when Reena sat down?
qa.a: Surprised and relieved to have someone kind beside her after eating alone.

grounding: Over several days a girl who envies a popular group refuses when they ask her to be cruel, and chooses kindness instead.

passage: 'Ayesha, you've been staring at those girls on the bus for a week. Let your Gurleen Aunty tell you a story. At your age, in Ludhiana, there was a group of girls everyone wanted to be with. They had the best tiffins and the loudest laughs. I wanted in so badly I dreamed about it. One day their leader said I could join, if I stopped wearing my kara and stopped speaking Punjabi at school, because it was "too village". I went home and stood at the mirror, turning the kara on my wrist. It was my grandmother's. The next morning I told them no. I cried in the washroom after. But by winter I had two friends who laughed at my Punjabi jokes, and I still have them now.'

qa.q: What did the leader ask young Gurleen to stop wearing?
qa.a: Gurleen's kara.

qa.q: What was young Gurleen feeling as she turned the kara at the mirror?
qa.a: Torn and sad; she badly wanted to belong, but the kara was her grandmother's and part of who she was.

qa.q: What choice in the story turned out wise, and why?
qa.a: Saying no to the group; the price was changing herself, and by winter she had friends who liked her as she was.

qa.q: How might the group's leader have seen Gurleen's refusal?
qa.a: Perhaps surprised or offended, since she was used to girls changing themselves to join.

grounding: An aunt recalls envying a popular group and refusing to join when the price was giving up who she was.
